title: Sindhudurg and the Maratha Navy
subtitle: How Shivaji Turned the Konkan Sea into a Wall of Swarajya
era: Coastal fort and navy building, 1664-1673 CE
region: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Kolaba, Khanderi and the Konkan coast from Daman toward Goa
moral: Sovereignty must defend its shores as carefully as its hills.

sources.citation: EIC Bombay and Surat Factory Records, 1670-1674, India Office Records, British Library
sources.note: Contemporary English monitoring of Maratha naval activity and fleet size.

sources.citation: Sabhasad Bakhar, tr. S.N. Sen, naval commanders and Sindhudurg traditions
sources.note: Names commanders including Daulat Khan and Maynak Bhandari.

sources.citation: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times, ch. 24, The Navy and Maritime Forts
sources.note: Classic study of fleet and sea forts.

sources.citation: Stewart N. Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818, pp. 79-85
sources.note: Critical assessment of a coastal navy built with Portuguese technical knowledge.

panels.shot: epic bird's‑eye wide of a rocky sea‑fort rising from waves, ships clustered around, Shivaji in the foreground cliffside, cloak whipping in the sea wind

dialogue.text: In an age when empires ruled from land, Shivaji Maharaj dared a new frontier: he carved Sindhudurg from the Konkan surf and built a coastal navy to shield Swarajya from sea‑borne powers.

panels.shot: slow push‑in from dark sea horizon toward a torchlit council chamber interior

dialogue.text: Through most Deccan wars, kings watched the sea like a distant line of ink. But along this inked line, Portuguese, Siddis and English ships decided who traded, who starved, who ruled.

panels.shot: wide shot of Konkan shoreline from above, ships off the coast, villages behind

dialogue.text: Sea‑borne cannon guarded Goa and Diu. Siddi fleets from Janjira raided markets and villages. European factors at Bombay and Surat watched, counting every new Maratha move with careful English ink.

panels.shot: medium close‑up on Shivaji, lit by a single oil lamp, eyes reflecting flame

dialogue.text: After the sack of Surat and clashes along the coast, one truth hardened in Shivaji’s mind: no Swarajya is safe if its shores are open. The hills had forts. The sea needed its own walls.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of rocky islet off Malvan coast with waves breaking around it

dialogue.text: Off Malvan, a ragged island of black laterite rock broke the waves. Tradition remembers 25 November 1664, when Shivaji chose this surf‑beaten stone as the seat of a new sea fort: Sindhudurg.

panels.shot: sweeping construction wide, showing hundreds of workers on the rocky islet

dialogue.text: For three years, engineers, stonecutters and boatmen worked between tide and storm. They carved ramparts into the rock, raised hidden gateways, and bound stone with lime that hardened under salty spray.

panels.shot: medium wide of a mixed group of officers before Shivaji on the fort platform

dialogue.text: He did not build this sea wall alone. Muslim officers like Daulat Khan and Darya Sarang, and Goan Christian pilots trained in Portuguese craft, brought tides, anchors and hulls into the language of Swarajya.

panels.shot: medium close‑up on Daulat Khan taking a command baton from Shivaji

dialogue.speaker: chhatrapati_shivaji_maharaj
dialogue.text: On land or sea, loyalty to Swarajya is our only wind.

panels.shot: dynamic wide of Konkan shipyards with half-built vessels on stocks

dialogue.text: Workshops along the creeks of Rajapur, Dabhol and beyond echoed with new craft. Maratha carpenters learned from coastal shipwrights to build lighter coastal vessels suited for sudden strikes and sheltering coves.

panels.shot: wide of a small squadron at sea hugging the shoreline, forts visible afar

dialogue.text: This was no deep‑ocean armada. It was a green‑water force, working close to shore, threading inlets and creeks, linking forts like Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg and Kolaba, and watching rival masts on the horizon.

panels.shot: sweeping coastal panorama showing Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg and Kolaba in sequence

dialogue.text: Stone by stone, fort by fort, a chain formed: Sindhudurg guarding Malvan, Vijaydurg watching the mid‑Konkan, Kolaba facing the waters near Bombay. Each became both harbour and shield.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle from a boat looking up at Sindhudurg’s massive walls

dialogue.text: Sindhudurg’s design was a message. From the sea, walls seemed sheer and unbroken. Within, sheltered anchorages allowed Maratha vessels to vanish from enemy eyes and burst forth when the tide favoured them.

panels.shot: wide of Siddi ships and Maratha craft eyeing each other at distance

dialogue.text: From Janjira, Siddi admirals tested these new walls. They probed coves, raided villages, and measured Maratha resolve. European diaries noted each encounter, counting guns, hulls and the changing balance along the coast.

panels.shot: medium shot of English factors in Bombay writing reports by candlelight

dialogue.text: Between 1670 and 1674, English records from Bombay and Surat watched this fleet with wary respect. They listed Maratha ships, forts, and movements in careful prose, proof that the Konkan sea was no longer idle.

panels.shot: medium interior of Sindhudurg bastion, Shivaji studying European-style cannon

dialogue.text: Shivaji learned from every shore he touched. Portuguese cannon casts, European rigging, Arab pilotage and Konkan seamanship fused in these forts. The sea turned from a foreign theatre into a familiar field of war.

panels.shot: nighttime wide of Khanderi island with campfires and anchored boats

dialogue.text: Northward, near Bombay, Khanderi became another testing ground. Contest over this rocky outpost with the English and Siddis showed that Maratha power now pressed not just inland ports, but key coastal gates.

panels.shot: close-up of Shivaji’s hand placing a small ship token on a map beside a fort token

dialogue.text: By the early 1670s, the map of Swarajya no longer stopped at the surf. Ships and forts were planned together. The same mind that had ringed the Sahyadris with stone now traced anchorages along the Konkan.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shivaji walking the ramparts of Sindhudurg at sunset

dialogue.speaker: chhatrapati_shivaji_maharaj
dialogue.text: If the sea stays ours, our children will not fear distant flags.

panels.shot: high wide shot pulling back from Sindhudurg to show coast and sea lanes fading into modern coastline

dialogue.text: Sindhudurg’s stones still taste salt. They remind us that sovereignty is not only a banner on a hilltop, but a watchful eye on every harbour, where waves can carry either trade or conquest to our doors.
